say: Quality and operations at volume.
This is the video for module 2 of Production Scaling and Quality Assurance.
When you make 20 items, your eyes catch most problems. When a team makes 2,000, problems slip through unless the process itself catches them.

say: Do not check everything. Pick critical characteristics: things the customer will notice, or that could harm someone. For a fried snack, that includes oil temperature, cooling and pack weight.
For each one, write the standard in numbers, the tool, and how often. For example, Kemi checks her oil is at 170 °C with a probe thermometer before every wok load.
Write who checks and signs the record.

The reaction plan is the column people forget. It has two parts: correct the product already made, and fix the process. If a pack is light, Kemi's packer holds the load, checks every pack, tops up, and tells the supervisor.
Keep it to one page, with a photo of the reference product beside it.
Mistake-proofing, called poka-yoke, designs the work so the error cannot happen, or is noticed at once. It works on every item, every time. Pre-weighed kits are one way.

For food, add hygiene to the plan: clean hands, surfaces and equipment, raw eggs kept apart, and hair covered. Write who checks, and when.

say: After switching to a fixed scoop, Ruth weighs 20 bags in the order she filled them.
The average, 1,010.05 g, is her centre line.
The moving range is the difference between each bag and the one before. Their average is 2.37 g.
The limits are the average plus or minus 2.66 times that, so 1,003.75 g to 1,016.35 g. Her lower limit now sits above the 1,000 g label claim.
She plots one bag every 30 minutes. One point outside a limit, or eight in a row on one side, means stop and find what changed.
With no signal, leave the process alone. Adjusting after every small difference adds variation.

panel.heading: Ruth's individuals chart
panel.rule: Control limits come from your data, not the specification.

say: Takt time is available time divided by customer demand. Kemi has 2,100 minutes a week, and shops want 2,000 packs. So one pack every 1.05 minutes.

panel.heading: Can Kemi make 2,000 packs a week?

say: Time each stage per load, then divide by packs per load. Mixing is 0.48 minutes a pack.

panel.heading: Can Kemi make 2,000 packs a week?

say: Rolling and cutting is 1.73, the slowest. Not frying, as Kemi expected. Her line makes only about 1,214 packs a week.

panel.heading: Can Kemi make 2,000 packs a week?

say: Frying, at 1.18, is also over takt.

panel.heading: Can Kemi make 2,000 packs a week?

say: She adds a hand-cranked dough sheeter and lights a second wok burner. Capacity rises to about 2,187 packs a week.
A faster mixer would not have helped at all.

panel.heading: Can Kemi make 2,000 packs a week?
panel.rule: Fix the slowest stage first. Buy equipment only for it.

say: First-pass yield is the share of units that pass every check the first time. Kemi's is 368 out of 400, which is 92%.

card.title: The true cost of a good pack

say: Her batch costs about 180,000 naira. Repacking 20 packs adds about 1,200.

card.title: The true cost of a good pack

say: That is 181,200 naira for 388 good packs, so 467 naira each, not the 450 she gets from the plan.
Over 2,000 packs a week, that gap is about 34,000 naira. So price from cost per good unit, never from the plan.

card.title: The true cost of a good pack

say: To remember. Write a one-page control plan with reactions. Make errors hard with mistake-proofing. Use charts to watch the process. Fix the bottleneck first. And price from cost per good unit.
